The words

Christ, whose glory fills the skies,
Christ, the true, the only Light,
Sun of Righteousness, arise,
Triumph o’er the shades of night;
Dayspring from on high, be near;
Day-star, in my heart appear.

Dark and cheerless is the morn
Unaccompanied by Thee;
Joyless is the day’s return
Till Thy mercy’s beams I see;
Till they inward light impart,
Glad my eyes, and warm my heart.

Visit then this soul of mine,
Pierce the gloom of sin and grief;
Fill me, Radiancy divine,
Scatter all my unbelief;
More and more Thyself display,
Shining to the perfect day.

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum D and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on s (A).
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t and the chromatic se. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

Charles Wesley published these words in 1740. The tune RATISBON comes from Werner’s Choralbuch (Leipzig, 1815), harmonised by William Henry Havergal in 1861.

  • Words (1740): Charles Wesley (1707–1788)
  • Melody (1815): Werner's Choralbuch
  • Harmony (1861): William Henry Havergal (1793–1870)

Tune RATISBON (WERNER) by William Henry Havergal (1793–1870); words by Charles Wesley (1707–1788).

Sung to the same tune: As the Hart, with Eager Looks, Ever Patient, Loving, Meek, It Is Finished! Glorious Word, Jesus, While He Dwelt Below, On Thy Church, O Power Divine, Praise to God, Immortal Praise, Quiet, Lord, My Froward Heart, Safely Through Another Week, Savior Shine and Cheer My Soul, When the Parting Bosom Bleeds, Who Shall Towards Thy Chosen Seat.

Questions about Christ, Whose Glory Fills the Skies

What is the doh of Christ, Whose Glory Fills the Skies?

In this version, in D major, doh is D. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does Christ, Whose Glory Fills the Skies start on?

It starts on s (A in D major). Find doh first, then sing up or down to s.

Is Christ, Whose Glory Fills the Skies in the public domain?

Yes. Charles Wesley died in 1788, William Henry Havergal died in 1870; the words were first published in 1740 and the music in 1815. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
